differences.title: 1. DELIVERY MODEL
differences.leftDesc: Kafka persists records into a replicated partition log; consumers track progress via offsets stored client-side or via commit APIs. Replays are driven by offset selection, enabling flexible rewind and multi-consumer independence.
differences.rightDesc: Kinesis stores data in sharded streams and exposes reads via iterators (e.g., Trim HORIZON or AFTER_SEQUENCE_NUMBER). Consumers manage iterator state externally; rewind depends on retention window and shard sequence numbers.

differences.title: 2. PARTITIONING UNIT
differences.leftDesc: Kafka scales by splitting topics into partitions; a partition is an ordered unit with a leader replica. Producers choose the target partition using partitioner logic or keys, controlling parallelism and ordering guarantees.
differences.rightDesc: Kinesis scales via shards, each providing an ordered sequence within the shard. Producers map records to a shard using the partition key; throughput capacity is allocated per shard, making shard planning central to performance.

differences.title: 3. RETENTION & REPLAY
differences.leftDesc: Kafka retains data based on time/size policies at the broker level, allowing long reprocessing horizons. Consumers can replay historical events as long as the segment files remain, limited by configured retention.
differences.rightDesc: Kinesis retention is bounded by a managed window (commonly up to 365 days, configurable within limits). Once trimmed, older records are not readable; replay is constrained by retention and iterator positioning.

differences.title: 4. REPLICATION & FAILOVER
differences.leftDesc: Kafka replicates each partition across multiple brokers (replication factor) with a leader coordinating writes and reads. Failover promotes an in-sync replica; the ISR set influences durability and acknowledged offsets.
differences.rightDesc: Kinesis handles underlying replication and failover internally as a managed service. You provision shard throughput, while AWS maintains the storage durability and availability semantics behind the scenes, exposing a simplified API surface.

differences.title: 5. PRODUCER BACKPRESSURE
differences.leftDesc: Kafka producer batching and acknowledgements (acks settings) regulate durability vs latency. When brokers are slow, client-side buffering and request retries create backpressure patterns that engineers can tune precisely.
differences.rightDesc: Kinesis enforces per-shard write capacity. If producers exceed throughput, writes are throttled, and your producer must handle ProvisionedThroughputExceededException via retries/backoff or batching within shard limits.

differences.title: 6. CONSUMER READ PERFORMANCE
differences.leftDesc: Kafka consumers fetch bytes from brokers using the fetch API; latency is impacted by fetch sizes, batching, and network round trips. Partition parallelism comes from consumer group assignment to partitions.
differences.rightDesc: Kinesis consumers retrieve records by iterating over shard data using managed iterators. Performance depends on shard count, iterator age, and polling/read patterns; scaling consumers typically means increasing shard-level parallel reads.

differences.title: 7. OPERATIONAL OWNERSHIP
differences.leftDesc: Running Kafka often means operating broker nodes, storage, monitoring, and scaling decisions (topic/partition strategy, replication factor). You trade operational effort for maximal control over architecture and costs.
differences.rightDesc: Kinesis offloads cluster operations to AWS: scaling, upgrades, and broker/storage management are handled for you. Engineers focus on stream design (partition keys, shard count) and consumption logic rather than infrastructure.
